sources.entry: Programmers should stop celebrating incompetence, DHH

summary.title: Programmers should stop celebrating incompetence
summary.one_liner: An opinion essay arguing that the programming community should stop glorifying copy-paste ignorance and instead encourage developers to pursue real understanding and mastery.
takeaways: Welcoming beginners should not require portraying programmers as clueless; the essay calls this a flawed prescription for imposter syndrome.
Copy-pasting solutions is a starting point, but developers should dig deeper to understand what the code actually does.
Influential experienced programmers should avoid presenting a know-nothing facade, since it discourages people from pursuing depth.
Mastery takes time and varies by person and domain, and it is fine to accept boundaries while still aiming for expertise.
Programming's apparent magic fades as you learn how the machine works, which is the path from bedazzled audience member to wizard.
summary.summary: The author, DHH, argues that the programming world has overcorrected against imposter syndrome and gatekeeping by celebrating incompetence and self-deprecation. He acknowledges the problems, noting that many programmers are self-taught, but says the proposed fix is wrong. He urges developers to treat copy-paste fixes as a step toward real understanding, and urges experienced programmers not to feign ignorance. The essay is a short opinion piece built on rhetoric and analogies (the wizard apprentice, the chess analogy) rather than data or code.
